title.en: Kumagdlat and Asalok: The Raid on the Erkileks
title.zh: 庫馬格拉克與阿薩洛克：襲擊厄基萊克族

region.en: Inland plain by a lake (legendary American-continent setting)
region.zh: 湖畔內陸平原（傳說中的美洲大陸故地）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from five Greenland copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three devoted cousins are split by a resentful old hag's lie, and Kumagdlat steals away with his boat, passing the settlements as a diving spotted seal by a seal-skull amulet — betrayed only by a clairvoyant fool. Reunited by chance under the setting sun, the cousins leap a stone's-throw to a refuge island, shoot the pregnant erkilek woman through the body, survive an arrow-storm (Merak's throat healed by Kumagdlat's life-restoring spell), destroy the tribe at their waterfall hiding-place, and carry home beautiful knives from copper-pot furnished tents — thanking the old bachelor who had kept Kumagdlat's family from starving.
summary.zh: 三位至親的表兄弟被老嫗的謊言離間；庫馬格拉克載家私夜遁，以海豹頭骨護符將船假作潛水斑豹，唯有先知般的愚者識破。日落時分兄弟重逢於高原，齊躍一石之遙登避難小島；夜襲厄基萊克帳——一箭射穿孕婦——箭雨中梅拉克喉傷，賴庫馬格拉克復生咒語而癒。瀑布藏匿處他以飛石盡殲其族，攜美柄寶刀而歸，並設宴致謝救其家人免於饑餓的老鰥夫。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads this tale as a memory of primeval Eskimo-Indian conflicts on the American continent and of earliest tool-culture (shells, stone, metal). Graphic violence recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Three cousins named Kumagdlat, Asalok, and Merak were very fond of one another; Kumagdlat kept a house and boat by himself, the other two in partnership, and they all assisted each other early and late, exercising and exhibiting their mutual strength. Kumagdlat had an old crone living with him, very cross-tempered; he warned her he would put her to death some day, and she behaved quietly until one day she exclaimed: 'It is not without reason that I am so quiet and low-spirited; from the first day thou beganst to maintain and support me I have been very sorry for thee... Is it not that thy cousins love thee so very dearly? Nevertheless they now intend to put an end to thy life.' She had invented this lie, being so ill-natured she could not even sleep at night — but from that time Kumagdlat began to fear his cousins, and began to shun them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Excusing himself twice that his kayak must dry, he loaded his boat and pushed off, telling the people on shore to tell his cousins to follow him out to their usual reserves. They returned, followed next morning — and found no marks or traces of him. Kumagdlat had the skull of a seal for an amulet: passing inhabited places he fixed it on the prow of his boat so the people would think it nothing but a spotted seal diving up and down; in one settlement a fool — fools being considered clairvoyants — cried 'A boat! a boat!' while the others could see only a diving seal, and from this news Asalok's party knew Kumagdlat must have passed. Travelling night and day, he stopped at a well-peopled place where a very old man was busily making a boat, his hair white as the side of an iceberg, a bearded young man beside him: 'Before this young man here was born I commenced building that boat, and by this time I have only just finished the hull' — his only tools being heaps of shells piled right and left. 'Here we have not got so much as a single knife; but yonder, in the interior of the country, live people who have knives in abundance... Farther inland numerous erkileks have their abodes, and they are immensely rich. However, when any of the coast people go there they never return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kumagdlat made himself a small bow and arrows, a quiver of seal-skin, and started for the erkileks all by himself; meanwhile the brothers Asalok and Merak, wandering long, discovered an extensive plain where the erkileks lived in many tents with only a lake for their sea. Hiding till nightfall, they espied under the setting sun a very tall man carrying a burden on his back — 'Why, is not that man like Kumagdlat?' — and the three, happily reunited, resolved that since they had met, one of the hateful erkileks should fall. Kumagdlat told his cousins how the old hag had calumniated them. In the dark they chose a small island right opposite the tents, a stone's-throw off, as a place of refuge; Kumagdlat, with the burden on his back, leaped first and gained the island, Asalok too, and Merak — though not without touching the water. Depositing all but two arrows each, they returned to the mainland, entered the largest tent, and through the skin curtain beheld an old married couple: the man, howling like a dog, licking the pregnant woman's belly as she handed him reindeer-tallow. 'Next time he begins to lick her, I'll take aim and shoot her' — and Kumagdlat shot her right through the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A fearful yell rose, and the cousins hurried across to the island, lying in a row, Kumagdlat in front, Merak hindmost. The erkileks armed and discharged arrows — the women pulling them from above discharged them much quicker than the men — and one whistling through the air struck Merak dangerously in the throat because he ventured to raise his head. 'Dost not thou know any spell for restoring life?' asked Asalok; Kumagdlat murmured words until the arrow had gone half-way out of Merak's throat, and at the third speaking Merak was alive and unhurt. When the erkileks had used up all their arrows, Kumagdlat had only the skin of his temple grazed; the cousins arose to pay them back with their bows, shot a great number, pursued the rest along a river to a waterfall hiding-place, and Kumagdlat killed them all by throwing stones as they issued forth one by one. The children who had remained immovable, feigning death, were caught and pierced through the ears and killed — only one boy and a girl left alive. The furniture of the erkileks held pots of copper with copper handles, and boxes whose covers unlocked of themselves with the quantity of clothes they contained; other boxes held knives with beautiful handles, of which they took as many as they could possibly carry, and made their way to the coast. There Kumagdlat's wife, mocked by neighbours crying that those who went to the erkileks never brought back beautiful knives, was believed a widow and kept from hunger by an old bachelor. Kumagdlat came descending the hill with great loads of hafted knives, thanked him — 'Having such great cause to be thankful towards him, I must have him come in' — and made him sit down and accept two of the knives. The cousins afterwards returned to their old home and grew very renowned for vigour and dexterity, killing bears as well as kilivfaks, the fabulous beasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.

title.en: Akigsiak: Son of the Coast and the Interior
title.zh: 阿基克夏克：海濱與內陸之子

region.en: Fiord head and inland country (legendary contact zone)
region.zh: 峽灣深處與內陸（傳說中的接觸地帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; six copies collated, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Carried off by an inlander as a bride, a coast woman bears Akigsiak, feared for strength among the inland folk though smaller of growth. In four reports to the coast people he tells of escaping the monstrous fat-bodied reptile of the north that he had earlier fled in a snowstorm; of luring a whale up the river by an old coast man's magic lay and sharing it with all; of a salmon-shaped giant fish hauled back across the river by a head-over-heels leap; of the pot-bearer igalilik he crushed down a precipice — and of the inorusek giant whose stone-throwing dare made him kill a passing kayaker, a deed of repentance after which he never ventured among the coast people again.
summary.zh: 海濱女子被內陸人擄為妻，生子阿基克夏克；他身量雖小，卻為內陸族所畏。他先後四次向海濱人自述：雪暴中誤遇北方巨蟒，几番跳越反擊，昏倒逃生，族人循跡剖其脂肉過冬；依老海濱人之咒歌引鯨入河、遍分其肉；又於窄河處翻躍對岸，從敵手奪回鮭形巨魚；以及他推下懸崖的負鍋巨人、與受石擲慫恿誤殺過路皮艇客的悔恨——自此他再不敢涉足海濱。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads this tale as referring to historical Eskimo-Indian contact. Killing of the kayaker recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: In days of yore some people went far into a firth to fish for salmon, and one of the women was carried off by an inlander to a very remote place; belonging to the coast people, she afterwards married her captor, and they begat a son named Akigsiak. In boyhood two of his father's nephews were his constant playfellows, but Akigsiak soon outdid them completely, even in swiftness; as his mother was of the coast people while his father was from the interior, he was smaller of growth, yet respected and feared by the other inlanders, with a great reputation for strength and ability in hunting. He sought intercourse with the coast people to gain information about his mother's relatives, and at such a meeting once told them: 'When my father grew older he was incapable of providing for us. One winter we had a great famine, and every day I went out in search of provisions; meanwhile my father watched me from the tops of the highest mountains, taking note of any change in the weather, and as soon as the sky darkened he made me a signal I could hear far and wide, after which I took my way homewards.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His father warned him he might go anywhere except to the north, because of a monstrous reptile reported to ravage those parts. One day the signal came before he had killed any game, and he did not obey it; the storm overtook him, and wandering blind in wind and snow-drift he discovered what appeared to be two large windows of a house, then that the other parts were like a hill — and finally that this was the terrible reptile his father had warned him against. He took to flight; the reptile had seen him and pursued, but whenever it came up he leapt across it, striking it with his lance. At last, it quite close upon him, he cried aloud with fatigue, fell to the ground, and lost his senses — to be awakened by a cool touch upon his face: the reptile lay close to his feet, unmoving. With his eyes constantly fixed on it he crept cautiously away, rose, and walked on, not reaching home until the fourth day, having been given up for lost. His father said their housemates had nothing to help him with, but he told how he had barely escaped the reptile, apparently leaving it dead — 'The body of the reptile is said to consist of nothing but fat,' said his father, adding that the house-fellows were almost starving. They went out in search of the monster; many died on the road before reaching the spot, but those who arrived flensed away at him and found him principally fat mixed with a little lean flesh, and had it for food the whole winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next time he told how, on an excursion with his father, they observed a whale close outside the sea-shore with a number of coast people standing on the beach; by his father's orders he ran down and made an old man teach him a magic lay for luring the whale up the river. As soon as the whale had entered the river a crowd of inlanders appeared, and before they could penetrate the whale's skin with their harpoons, Akigsiak ran home to fetch his weapons — rounding three large bays on the way — and returned in good time to despatch the whale, giving everybody his share, not forgetting the old coast man, whom he protected against the inlanders. At the third meeting he told how, hearing that other inlanders had caught an immense fish shaped like a salmon, he hurried to the river-side and threw his harpoon into it too, but his companions being too few, the inlanders on the opposite side hauled it from them; he hastened to where the river was narrower, and in jumping across hurled himself round, head over heels, alighting on his feet on the opposite shore — where he frightened away the other inlanders, took his share of the fish, threw it across to his own people, and jumped back the same way. At the fourth meeting he told of a quarrel with an igalilik — a pot-bearer, one of the fabulous inlanders who carry boiling pots on their shoulders — whom he pushed down a precipice, crushing him to death against the rocks. At last Akigsiak met an inorusek, another kind of gigantic inlander, on the high banks of a river; amusing themselves throwing stones, the inorusek persuaded him to try to hit a kayaker passing below, whom he did not fail to kill on the spot. Repenting his deed, he afterwards slew the inorusek, but is said never from this time to have ventured among the coast people again, because of the murder — only once visiting a coast man on a river-bank to try a boxing-match and a race. Though said to be smaller than the other inlanders, he was at all events larger than our people: his back as broad as two others put together, his height very little less than two people on top of each other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Friends Who Poisoned Each Other

region.en: Outermost island and fiord head, West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭外島與峽灣深處

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; famous Greenland story, compiled from three copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 6 'The Friends', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two childhood friends regale each other with reindeer tallow and dried seal — until the fiord hunter lingers too long, the seals spoil, and the islander rubs corpse-fat on the cold dish to do him an evil turn. Warned by his tornak to turn the piece over, the angakok-guest escapes madness; but his own counter-poison strikes home, and the friend goes raving mad, eats up the inmates of his house, pursues him shore to shore and even walks on water to seize the kayak, until he is found dead in a cave, eyelids filled with blood, and the survivor closes the cave and is henceforth friendless.
summary.zh: 兩位青梅竹馬的摯友以馴鹿脂油與乾海豹互相款待——直到峽灣獵手遲遲不歸，海豹腐壞，島上的他於冷盤海豹上抹屍脂害友。友人是巫師，靈助示警令其翻轉肉片逃過瘋狂；然而反毒計中的獵手終於發狂，吞食全家，追友於海陸之間，甚至踏水抓艇。最後在岩洞中尋見他：蜷縮而死，眼瞼充滿血。倖存者封閉洞口，從此孤身無友。

sensitivity.note: Rink compiled three copies. The corpse-fat poisoning motif is a documented Greenlandic sorcery belief; madness and death recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Two friends loved each other very dearly, constant companions from childhood; one lived at one of the outermost islands, the other far up at the head of a fiord. They visited each other often, and when parted for some days felt a mutual longing to meet again. In summer the fiord man went reindeer-hunting in the interior, always taking back a whole reindeer with velvety horns and all the tallow in it to regale his friend; the islander, on his part, saved large quantities of seals, and when the hunter returned was regaled with nicely-dried seal-flesh, while in the evening the frozen meat was set before him as a cold dish — the guest praising it very much, gossiping till late. The next day the islander visited in return, ate reindeer-flesh and especially the tallow till he was ready to burst, and was presented with dried meat and tallow at his departure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 6 'The Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One autumn the hunter lingered in the interior longer than usual; the earth was quite frozen over and still he did not return. The friend longed for him, then grew angry, and when the first preserved seals began to spoil they commenced eating away at the whole lot. Hearing the hunter had returned, he went out to a grave, cut a bit of fat from a dead body, and with it rubbed certain parts of a seal he intended to treat his friend with, to do him an evil turn on his arrival. The meeting was pleasant and the regale as usual; the hunter explained his long absence — small luck in getting reindeer with velvety horns — and the host answered that when his first preserved seals began to rot they had eaten them all up, adding, 'Let us have the one that was last put by; we will have it for a cold dish.' He laid the piece rubbed over with corpse-fat uppermost and begged his friend to partake; but as the visitor was helping himself, something from beneath the ledge gave a pull at his leg — twice — and he went outside. Being an angakok, the voice of his tornak warned him: 'Thy friend regales thee with a base design; turn the piece over when thou goest back and eat of the opposite part; if thou eatest of the part that is now uppermost thou wilt be sure to go mad.' He turned the meat over; his host thought it a mere accident. The guest felt a pain in his stomach — he had probably touched some of the poisoned flesh — but soon recovered, and on taking leave asked his friend to return the visit soon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 6 'The Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he came home he took a reindeer with velvety horns, treated it as his friend had done the seal, rubbing it well with fat from a dead body; and when his guest came, regaled him with dried meat and tallow, never before so much to his taste. At night the reindeer was set before them with the poisoned side turned up — 'There, we have got some cold meat; I have kept it for thee this long while' — and the friend ate away, exclaiming several times, 'This is really delicious!' 'Yes, that is because it is so very fat,' the host answered. When the meal was over the guest felt a pain in his stomach, looked hard at everyone present, went outside, and the pains were not relieved. It was a long time before the host saw him again; at last, when ice covered the waters, the friend's boat put into the firth without him: 'He is ill, and has turned raving mad; he wanted to eat us, and therefore we all took flight.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 6 'The Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the huntsman went to visit his friend: nobody about the house, but creeping through the entry he beheld him lying on his back, eyes staring wildly, head hanging over the edge of the couch. He went up and asked how he did, but no answer came — then his friend suddenly started up and shouted with all his might: 'Because thou hast feasted me basely, I have eaten up all the inmates of my house, and I will now devour thee too' — and bounded towards him. The visitor escaped through the entry to his kayak, pushing off as the pursuer was in the very act of seizing hold of him. The madman ran along the shore crying, quite sensibly, 'I feel much better now; do come back. When I have not seen thee for a day or two, I am longing dreadfully for thee' — and the friend believed him, put back, and had to push off again as the rush came. At home he neither spoke nor ate from grief; his housemates advised him never to return, sure the madman would eat him too. Nevertheless, next morning he paddled away as if compelled. The madman pursued him right into the house, fastening the door so he had to get out through the window; the next day he found his friend worse — lying with his head on the floor and heels on the bench, eyes far protruded, the bone of his nose as sharp as a knife's edge — and was pursued round the room, 'I am starving; I must have thee for food,' escaping at last by the window. Getting clear of the shore, he saw the madman walking on the surface of the water ready to seize the prow; swinging to and fro in his kayak he raised ripples so the madman could not steady himself, very nearly falling, and so escaped him once more. The day after, his housemates again tried to detain him — 'When I have not seen my friend for a whole day, I am ready to die with longing, and cannot desist from going to him' — but the house was deserted; some footprints wound up the hills to a cave in the rock, where his friend sat bent together and much shrunk. Trying to lift him, he found him quite dead, his eyelids filled with blood; he carefully covered and closed up the entrance of the cave, and was henceforth friendless.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 6 'The Friends'; not verbatim.

title.en: Katerparsuk: The Boy in the Walrus Skin
title.zh: 卡特帕舒克：披海象皮的少年

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; commonly known all over Greenland, constructed from five manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 7 'Katerparsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: No one will lend the orphan Katerparsuk a knife, so he builds his kayak with stone tools and shells — and the wicked man of the place terrifies him in a bear-skin for the fun of it. Mortally vexed, the boy studies angakok science and perfects a magic lay that makes a walrus throw off its skin; sliding into it, he hardens it against harpoons, snatches the old tormentor's harpoon, line, and bladder-float, and at a feast hangs them up before the boaster: 'Look, there are all thy hunting tools.' The fun of playing walrus to the man who had played bear appeases his resentment.
summary.zh: 無人肯借刀給孤兒卡特帕舒克，他以石器和貝殼自製皮艇；同村的惡棍卻披熊皮嚇他取樂。少年憤而修習巫術，練成令海象蛻皮的咒歌——鑽入海象皮中硬化抗叉，奪走老惡棍的魚叉、獵繩與浮囊。宴會上他把這些工具懸在牆上：『看，你的全套獵具，回去時帶走吧。』以海象之身回敬熊皮之戲，他的怨恨才算平息。

sensitivity.note: Rink constructed this version from five manuscripts. Walrus-skin magic is a documented Greenlandic wizard feat.

passages.text: Katerparsuk was a poor orphan boy who, growing up, was anxious to get on in the world because nobody wanted to take care of him. Resolving to make himself a kayak by his own efforts, and nobody willing to lend him a knife, he first tried stone tools and later shells. In the same place lived a wicked man who, instead of pitying the poor boy, took delight in annoying and terrifying him: disguising himself in a bear-skin, he stole up behind Katerparsuk growling like a bear, and the boy flung down his work and tools in consternation and ran away. The other house-fellows, coming to the spot and seeing his implements of shells and stones, were quite moved at the sight; meanwhile the wicked man came forward: 'Instead of pitying thee I scorned thee; because thou, silly boy, couldst ever think of making a kayak all by thyself: and that was why I frightened thee in a bear-skin.' The housemates broke out into laughter at the poor boy's embarrassment, but he grew mortally vexed, thinking only of revenge and resentment, and betook himself to solitary places to study angakok science.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 7 'Katerparsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After a long time he finished his kayak, exercised himself in rowing and hunting, and was soon able to hunt seals. Having once seen a walrus dive from the top of a hill, he thought, 'Oh that I could make him throw off his skin!' He began to sing a magic lay without result, went home much dissatisfied, and did not rest till he had got up an incantation to suit his purpose, first trying it successfully on a hare. One day, when all the hunters were away in their kayaks, he rowed out to a remote place, ascended a very high hill with a view of the sea, detected many walrus diving up and down, and sang his magic lay to one of them until it approached the beach right below him — singing louder and louder until the animal at last threw off its skin. Katerparsuk crept into it at once, tried swimming and diving, and when the kayakers approached knew how to harden his skin so the harpoon could not pierce it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 7 'Katerparsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile the wicked man had grown old and decrepit and given up seal-hunting, going out only to fish. Once Katerparsuk put on his walrus-skin and emerged from the water close to the old man's fishing-place, hearing him exclaim, 'Oh that I were young again, what a catch I might have had!' The old man returned home, collected all his hunting implements unused for a long time, and took them out to his fishing-place next day: 'Oh, look! there he is again!' — paddling towards him. Katerparsuk hardened his skin and made it tough, seized the point of the harpoon, pulled it down into the water along with the hunting-bladder, took out the stopper so the air escaped, and hurried home in his kayak. The old man was vexed at losing his bladder-float and boasted at home: 'I have again commenced to go out hunting; to-day I pursued a large walrus, but he escaped me, and took my bladder-float along with him.' Katerparsuk let him chat on, but in the evening invited all the men to a feast, the old man of the party; after the meal, when the boaster had told his tale again, Katerparsuk pointed to the bladder-float and harpoon-line hung on a peg in the wall: 'Look, there are all thy hunting tools, and thou canst take them away with thee when thou goest home.' And the old man looked quite abashed, and left the party in a somewhat confused state. It is said that the resentment of Katerparsuk was somewhat appeased by the fun he had had in playing walrus to the man who had been playing bear to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 7 'Katerparsuk'; not verbatim.
